'''''Oenanthe lachenalii''''', '''parsley water-dropwort''', is a [[flowering plant]] in the [[Apiaceae|carrot family]], which is native to [[Europe]] and parts of [[North Africa]]. It is a declining plant of coastal [[wetland]]s.

==Description==

Parsley water-dropwort is a hairless [[perennial]] growing up to 100 cm tall with solid (sometimes becoming hollow with age), striated, cylindrical stems 0.4 cm in diameter. The roots are somewhat swollen, cylindrical in shape, but lacking the distinct [[tuber]]s that occur in some other members of the genus. The upper leaves are once to twice [[pinnate]] with simple linear leaflets up to 5 cm long; the lower ones are twice pinnate, with wider, flat leaflets, more like those of other [[Apiaceae|umbellifers]]. The [[petiole (botany)|leaf stalks]] are shorter than the leaf blade, sheathing the stem at the base, and with a celery scent.<ref name=Tutin>{{cite book |last1=Tutin |first1=T.G. |title=Umbellifers of the British Isles |date=1980 |publisher=Botanical Society of the British Isles |location=London}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Poland |first1=John |last2=Clement |first2=Eric |title=The Vegetative Key to the British Flora |date=2009 |publisher=John Poland |location=Southampton |isbn=978-0-9560144-0-5}}</ref>

It flowers between June and September in northern Europe, with [[umbels]] of 5-9 smaller umbels about 1-2 cm in diameter, each of which has numerous white flowers. There are about 5 awl-shaped [[bract]]s on the main umbel and 5-7 small bracteoles at the base of each of the individual umbellules. Plants are monoecious, with [[hermaphrodite|hermaphroditic]] and male flowers in all umbels, but the proportion of hermaphroditic flowers decreases as the season progresses. Each flower has 5 unequal [[petal]]s with the larger, outer ones slightly larger, 5 [[stamen]]s and 2 prominent [[Stigma (botany)|styles]] arising from a swollen base (stylopodium) at the top of the ovary. After flowering, the flower stalks do not expand (as they do in some other species of [[Oenanthe (plant)|water-dropwort]]) and the umbels do not become flat-topped.<ref name="Tutin" /><ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref>
[[File:Oenanthe lachenalii.jpeg|thumb|Flowers of parsley water-dropwort]]

==Identification==
This species is very similar to [[Oenanthe silaifolia|narrow-leaved water-dropwort]], to the extent that there is often confusion between them. In general, they should be easy to distinguish: parsley water-dropwort usually has bracts on the main umbels, the rays do not thicken after flowering, and the umblets do not become flat-topped in fruit. However, some plants lack bracts and could be difficult to identify in flower. Usually, parsley water-dropwort will have broader (parsley-like) leaflets on the lower leaves early in the year. The best way to confirm identification is from the mature fruit, which are winged in parsley water-dropwort and only ridged in the other species.<ref name="Tutin" />
[[File:Oenanthe lachenalii bracts.jpg|thumb|A fresh umbel, showing the bracts]]

==Taxonomy==
The first description of parsley water-dropwort was by the German botanist [[Karl Christian Gmelin]] in his ''Flora Badensis Alsatica''<ref>[https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/83758202 Flora Badensis Alsatica] OCLC WorldCat</ref> in 1805. It has many synonyms (i.e. other authors have subsequently named the same plant, but Gmelin's name has precedence), including ''O. approximata'' Mérat (1812), ''O. foucaudii'' Tess. (1891) ''Phellandrium tabernaemontani'' Bubani (1899). A full list can be found in the Synonymic Checklists of the Plants of the World.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hassler |first1=M. |title=Catalogue of Life Checklist |date=2023 |publisher=ChecklistBank |doi=10.48580/ddz4x-3dd |url=https://www.gbif.org/dataset/be1f0e7a-0ee0-45a8-847c-9d12e3997425 |access-date=12 March 2022}}</ref> A few forms and varieties have also been named, but none is currently accepted.

It is not known to hybridise with any other species.<ref name="Stace" />
[[File:Œnanthe de Lachenal - feuille inférieure.jpg|thumb|Lower leaf of parsley water-dropwort]]
[[File:Oenanthe lachenalii roots.jpg|thumb|The roots are slightly swollen but do not bear distinct tubers]]

The generic name ''[[Oenanthe (plant)|Oenanthe]]'', which comes from the [[Ancient Greek]] οίνος, "wine" and άνθος, "flower", was used in ancient times for certain Mediterranean plants and later adopted to describe this genus. The "dropwort" part of the common name is a reference to the tubers produced amongst the roots of certain other species in the [[Oenanthe (plant)|genus]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wiktionary |title=dropwort |date=16 January 2023 |url=https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/dropwort}}</ref>

Its chromosome number is 2n = 22 (based on British specimens).<ref name="Tutin" />

==Distribution and status==
The global range of parsley water-dropwort is in [[Western Europe]] as far as [[Poland]] and [[Greece]], extending northwards to southern [[Scandinavia]] and southwards as far as the coast of [[Africa]]. It is not recorded as an introduction beyond its natural range.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Global Biodiversity Information Facility |title=Oenanthe lachenalii C.C. Gmel. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/5540332}}</ref>
[[File:Oenanthe lachenalii stem.jpg|thumb|The petioles barely clasp the strongly ribbed stem]]

In Britain, it is classified as Least Concern, meaning that it is not rare nor declining at a particularly high rate.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cheffings |first1=C.M. | last2=Farrell |first2=L. |title=The Vascular Plant Red Data List for Great Britain |date=2005 |publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee |location=Peterborough}}</ref> It is, however, under threat, especially inland. In England, it has been assessed as decreasing by 24% between 1969 and 1999, and in one English county, Kent, by as much as 41%, although it is still not scarce. Causes of decline include drainage of wetlands and agricultural intensification.<ref name="Atlas" /><ref>{{cite book |last1=Kitchener |first1=G.D. |title=Kent Rare Plant Register |date=2021 |url=https://bsbi.org/wp-content/uploads/dlm_uploads/rare-plant-register-accounts-O-Oe-Orc-Feb-2021.pdf}}</ref> 

It is considered an [[axiophyte]] in any British county.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |title=Axiophytes |url=https://bsbi.org/axiophytes}}</ref>

In France, it is widespread and classified as Least Concern, indicating that populations are generally stable, overall. However, it is rare and threatened in some inland régions such as [[Alsace]], where it is Critically Endangered (CR) and [[Île-de-France]] (Endangered, EN). In the [[Auvergne]] it is thought to be extinct, or 'locally extirpated'.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Inventaire National du Patrimoine Naturel |title=Œnanthe de Lachenal |url=https://inpn.mnhn.fr/espece/cd_nom/109881 |access-date=19 May 2022}}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
This is a wetland plant, occurring primarily in slightly brackish grassland close to the coast. It is also found in freshwater inland marshes, particularly in France and Spain. In Britain, its ecological preferences are described as varying from the upper part of salt marshes, through brackish dykes to base-rich fen-meadows inland. It is fairly common around the coast of both Britain and Ireland, with the exception of northern and eastern Scotland.<ref name=Atlas>{{cite book |last1=Preston |first1=C.D. |last2=Pearman |first2=D.A. |last3=Dines |first3=T.D. |title=New Atlas of the British and Irish Flora |date=2002 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford |url=https://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/plant/oenanthe-lachenalii |archive-date=2022-03-12 |access-date=2022-03-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220312103551/https://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/plant/oenanthe-lachenalii |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Its [[Indicator value|Ellenberg values]] in Britain are L = 8, F = 8, R = 8, N = 5, and S = 3.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hill|first1=M.O.|last2=Mountford|first2=J.O.|last3=Roy|first3=D.B.|last4=Bunce|first4=R.G.H.|title=Ellenberg's indicator values for British plants. ECOFACT Volume 2. Technical Annex|date=1999|publisher=Institute of Terrestrial Ecology|isbn=1870393481|url=http://nora.nerc.ac.uk/6411/1/ECOFACT2a.pdf|accessdate=29 May 2017}}</ref>

In the [[Aiguamolls de l'Empordà]], in Spain, studies show that it occurs in a variety of habitats, from [[Festuca arundinacea|tall fescue]]/[[Hordeum secalinum|meadow barley]] meadows with [[Apium graveolens|wild celery]], [[Juncus gerardii|saltmarsh rush]] and [[Lotus tenuis|narrow-leaved bird's-foot trefoil]], to wetter [[Paspalum distichum|water finger-grass]]/[[Carex divisa|divided sedge]] grassland and through to brackish marsh with [[Polypogon monspeliensis|annual beard-grass]], [[Tripolium pannonicum|sea aster]] and [[Juncus subulatus|Somerset rush]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Watt |first1=S. |last2=Vilar |first2=L. |title=A comparative study of the vegetation at Aiguamolls de l'Emporda wetlands (N.E. Iberian peninsula) |journal=Scientia Gerundensis |volume=23 |pages=109–154 |url=https://www.raco.cat/index.php/Scientia/article/download/45569/55133}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Watt |first1=S.C.L. | last2=García-Berthou |first2=E. | last3=Vilar|first3=L. |title=The influence of water level and salinity on plant assemblages of a seasonally flooded Mediterranean wetland |journal=Plant Ecology |date=2007 |volume=189 |pages=71–85 |doi=10.1007/s11258-006-9167-7|s2cid=13816485 }}</ref>

==Uses==
Although it can be a component of hay meadows, parsley water-dropwort is considered to be poisonous to livestock, albeit not as toxic as [[Oenanthe crocata|hemlock water-dropwort]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=West |first1=G.P. |title=Black's Veterinary Dictionary |date=1998 |publisher=Barnes & Noble Books |isbn=9780389210177 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rxAD2cWqYI0C}}</ref> No part of the plant is edible by humans, and it appears to have no commercial uses.
